title: Another Year Here...
author: Lance Eaton
summary: For the third anniversary of his AI+Edu=Simplified Substack, Lance Eaton had Claude interview him one question at a time, drawing on his full archive, and published the exchange. He argues that year 2 of agentic AI is repeating year 2 of generative AI, with institutions slow to understand what is being asked of them, and that refusal is negligent when students are already using AI heavily. He defends experiential engagement by invoking Dewey, while insisting that foundational skills still come first in some courses and that slowing down is different from refusing. On agentic tools he distinguishes efficiency from learning, imagining a student-built "learner’s workbench" and placing the line where an agent does the reading or learning for the student. He also reflects on interviews as applied classroom examples, his AI-use boundaries by context, the tension between a tapestry and a hustle mindset, and practical advice for would-be Substack writers. The piece is partly meta, but its higher-ed AI positions are substantive.
points: Eaton warns that higher education is replaying the slow, selective response to generative AI as agentic AI arrives, and asks whether institutions can keep up.
He rejects blanket refusal as negligent, since students are already using AI regularly, while accepting that foundational skills sometimes need to be built before AI is introduced.
The test for agentic AI in learning is whether it supports connections and removes friction or does the reading and thinking for the student.
A practical first assignment for skeptics is to have AI produce an output and then have students scrutinise it against the course content.
His own AI-use line shifts with context: interviewing and challenging for reflective writing, heavier drafting help for slides and communications, always with human refinement.
quotes: It deeply worries me that year 2 of agentic AI is playing out very much like year 2 of generative AI. I don’t know that institutions, departments, or really any of us understand the ask that this represents.

We have spent the last 20 or 30 years, even longer if you go back to John Dewey, talking about how experience matters, as opposed to abstract approaches. Responding to AI by just talking about it but not exploring it directly feels strange.

The agent stops supporting the learning and does the learning for the student when it’s doing the actual reading or engaging with the learning content, bypassing the student’s own interaction with it.
Given that, yes, there are places we want to slow down, but slowing down is different from refusal.

my recommendation for a skeptical educator reading this is to use AI to create outputs, or have students create outputs with AI, and then scrutinize them in a way that also reinforces the subject matter of the course.

What agentic AI represents as a tool of efficiency versus a tool of learning feels really hard to figure out. I want to explore what it could mean to have agentic tools in our teaching and learning spaces that enhance or expand meaningful ways to teach and learn beyond efficiency.
I think about the Substack less as a storefront and more as an archive, and it has always been set up that way.
